blocks.title: Forces
blocks.md: A **force** is a push or a pull, a vector measured in **newtons (N)**. The **resultant** of forces in a line: add forces in the same direction and subtract opposite ones: 10 N to the right and 4 N to the left give **6 N to the right**. **Weight** W = m × g is the gravitational force on a mass (g = 10 N/kg). **Friction** opposes motion and acts along the surfaces; it is larger on rough surfaces.

blocks.caption: Extension of a spring against force: straight line up to the elastic limit.
blocks.alt: A graph of force against extension: a straight line from the origin to 16 N at 8 cm, then a flatter curve beyond the limit.

blocks.title: Hooke's law
blocks.md: Within the **elastic limit**, the **extension of a spring is proportional to the force**: **F = k × x**, where k is the **spring constant** (N/cm or N/m). The graph is a straight line through the origin; its gradient is k. Beyond the **elastic limit** the spring does not return to its original length.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Extension is the **increase** in length, not the total length: extension = new length − natural length.
- Hooke's law does not work beyond the elastic limit.
- Weight is a force in N; mass is in kg.

blocks.title: Spring constant
blocks.statement: A spring stretches by 4.0 cm when a force of 8.0 N is applied. Find k, and the extension for 10 N (within the limit).

blocks.title: Resultant force
blocks.statement: A cart is pushed forward with 120 N while friction pulls back with 45 N. Find the resultant force.
steps: The forces are in opposite directions: subtract.

lessons.title: Newton's laws of motion
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Physics — Forces, Hooke's law, Newton's laws, moments (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State Newton's three laws of motion.
Use F = ma to find force, mass or acceleration.
Explain inertia and action-reaction pairs in everyday situations.
reviewNotes: Newton's laws are stated in a simplified student form; check the wording used by the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The three laws
blocks.md:
**First law**: an object stays at rest, or moves at constant velocity in a straight line, **unless an unbalanced force acts** on it. This property is **inertia**.

**Second law**: the resultant force produces an acceleration in its own direction: **F = m × a**.

**Third law**: if body A exerts a force on B, then B exerts an **equal and opposite force** on A. The two forces act on **different bodies**.

blocks.caption: Forces on a car: the resultant forward force makes it accelerate.
blocks.alt: A car with arrows: engine force 3000 N forward, friction 800 N backward, weight downward and reaction of the road upward.

blocks.title: Using F = ma
blocks.md: **F = ma** with F in newtons, m in kilograms and a in m/s². Then a = F ÷ m and m = F ÷ a. **F is the resultant (net) force**: add up all the forces along the line of motion first. **1 N** is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Use the **resultant** force, not just the engine force; friction must be subtracted.
- The two forces of the third law act on **different objects**, so they do not cancel each other.
- An object in motion does not need a continuing force to keep moving at constant velocity.

blocks.title: Acceleration of a car
blocks.statement: A car of mass 1000 kg has an engine force of 3000 N and a friction force of 800 N. Find its acceleration and its speed after 5 s from rest.

blocks.title: Inertia in a bus
blocks.statement: Passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly. Explain, using Newton's first law.
steps: Passengers were moving with the bus, and no force acts on them to stop.
The bus slows but their bodies tend to keep moving forward: inertia.
blocks.answer: Their inertia keeps them moving forward when the bus stops.

blocks.title: Moment of a force
blocks.md: The **moment** of a force about a pivot is its turning effect: **moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot**, unit **newton metre (N m)**. A longer spanner or a door handle far from the hinges needs a smaller force for the same moment. Moments can be **clockwise** or **anticlockwise**.

blocks.caption: A balanced beam: 40 N at 0.50 m on the left and an unknown force F at 0.25 m on the right.
blocks.alt: A beam resting on a pivot with a 40 N weight 0.50 m to the left and a force F 0.25 m to the right.

blocks.title: Principle of moments and equilibrium
blocks.md: For a body in **equilibrium** (balanced): **sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments** about any pivot, and **total upward force = total downward force**. The **centre of gravity** is the point where the whole weight seems to act; a uniform rod's is at its middle.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Use the **perpendicular** distance from the pivot to the line of the force, not the length of the beam.
- Remember the pivot supports the beam: its upward reaction equals all the downward forces.
- Convert cm to m before multiplying to get N m.

blocks.title: Balanced beam
blocks.statement: On a beam balanced at its pivot, a 40 N weight is 0.50 m to the left and a force F is 0.25 m to the right. Find F and the force on the pivot (beam weight ignored).
steps: Anticlockwise = 40 × 0.50 = 20 N m. At balance 0.25 × F = 20, so F = 80 N.
Reaction at the pivot = 40 + 80 = 120 N upward.

blocks.title: Crowbar
blocks.statement: A crowbar of effort arm 1.2 m and load arm 0.3 m is used. An effort of 60 N is applied. What load can it just lift?
